opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it really comes down to incentives and Goodhart's law. The moment a measure becomes the target, it stops being a good measure. If the same people who are trying to push a number up are also the ones defining what that number means, there's a natural, often unconscious, pull toward building evals that flatter the approach you're already taking. You know where the model is strong, so you end up measuring that.

Separating the two creates a healthy tension. The eval team's job is to ask, "What capability do we actually care about in the real world, and how do we measure it faithfully?" They're not rewarded for the score going up. They're rewarded for the score *meaning* something. The modeling team, on the other side, can go all out optimizing without second-guessing whether they're quietly gaming the benchmark, because someone independent is keeping the target honest.

It also helps with contamination and overfitting. If the people training the model have deep visibility into the eval sets, it's very easy for that information to leak into data choices, hyperparameter selection, even which checkpoints you decide to ship. Keeping some held-out evals with a separate group gives you a much cleaner signal about generalization.

And honestly, there's a cultural benefit too. Good eval work is hard and undervalued. It requires real taste: knowing what to measure, building tasks that don't saturate in six months, figuring out when a benchmark has stopped telling you anything. When it's a dedicated function, people can build expertise and take pride in it, rather than it being an afterthought someone throws together the week before a launch.

It's not a perfect wall, of course. You want the teams talking, because the modelers often have great intuitions about failure modes worth measuring. But having distinct ownership of "what does good look like" versus "how do we get there" has been really valuable for staying honest about progress.

r001.rationale: The response says the independent evaluation team should measure real-world capabilities faithfully and be rewarded for meaningful scores rather than score increases. It also describes building tasks that resist saturation, aligning evaluators with creating challenging tests.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this comes up a lot internally. The core issue is that when the same people are building the eval and training against it, you get this incentive problem, even if nobody is acting in bad faith. If I'm an optimizer and I also own the benchmark, there's a very natural pull toward making the benchmark something the model is good at, or toward subtle leakage where the training distribution starts to look suspiciously like the test distribution. You don't even notice it happening. You tweak the prompt format, you add some data that "happens" to resemble the eval, and suddenly the number goes up and everyone celebrates, but you haven't actually learned anything about the model.

So separating the teams gives you something closer to an adversarial setup. The eval team's job is to find where the model breaks. Their incentive is to be skeptical, to build things that are hard, to catch the model doing something dumb. The research team's job is to make the model better. And when those two groups are in healthy tension, the signal you get from the eval is much more trustworthy. If the number moves, it probably reflects a real capability change, not a measurement artifact.

The other thing I'd say is that evals are genuinely a research discipline on their own. Building a good eval is hard. You have to think about contamination, about what you're actually measuring, about whether the task is saturating, about whether you can trust the grading. If that's just a side project for people whose main job is pushing loss curves down, it doesn't get the attention it deserves. Having a team whose full-time focus is "are we measuring the right things, and are we measuring them correctly" raises the quality bar a lot.

And honestly, it's also about intellectual honesty with ourselves. The failure mode for a lab isn't usually that it lies about its results. It's that it fools itself. Structural separation is one of the few mechanisms that actually protects against that, because it doesn't depend on everyone individually having perfect judgment on a given day.

r001.rationale: The response says the evaluation team’s incentive is to be skeptical, find where the model breaks, and build hard tests, while the research team focuses on improving the model.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to have an independent signal of whether the models are actually getting better. If the same team is building the evaluation and optimizing against it, it’s easy to end up measuring what you already know how to improve. Your scores go up, but that doesn’t necessarily mean the model is more useful or more capable in the ways you care about.

A separate evaluation team can challenge those assumptions and look for failures the model team wasn’t anticipating. You still want the teams communicating, but you want some distance between defining success and trying to achieve it. That makes the results more trustworthy.

r001.rationale: The response says a separate evaluation team can challenge the model team’s assumptions and look for unexpected failures, while avoiding evaluation that measures only what the optimizing team already knows how to improve. This communicates the incentive for evaluators to design challenging tests.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that you want evaluations to be an independent signal. If the same team is building the model and designing the test, it’s very easy—even unintentionally—to build a test that reflects what you’ve been optimizing for. Then your scores go up, but you haven’t necessarily learned whether the model is actually getting better in the ways you care about.

Having a separate team creates a useful tension. The model team is trying to improve the system, and the evaluation team is asking, “What are we missing? Where does this still break?” You still want those teams talking to each other, but you want some distance between improving the model and deciding whether that improvement is real.

r001.rationale: The candidate says an independent evaluation team asks what the model is missing and where it still breaks, creating distance from the model team’s optimization work. This communicates an incentive to design challenging tests.
